items.title: Design/Implement on-boarding and a relay giving "face"
items.box:
Andy, 2026-10-19: "This goal is now really about folding relay and face into one.... it will come with a lot of shell fixes later......"

DECIDED
- Secrets stay on the node, in relay-state/, never served to a page, never in git. No encryption at rest.
- Providers are a generic dataset, plugins only where a provider needs its own flow. Each provider record carries its help in prose with links to where the key is obtained.
- Andy, 2026-10-19: "we don't need a keys app."
- An app never sees a key: it asks the node to call provider X, the node attaches the credential and returns the answer only. Granted per app and per provider.
- Only Andy adds, changes or removes a key or connects an OAuth account, from his own session.
- Only the relay/face owner holds the OAuth agreements with the login providers; a member needs none. The home node never sees an OAuth flow: its face says this verified email is you.
- A member chooses a name one level under the relay domain (andy.noderoutes.net), tied to their verified email. One wildcard DNS record and one wildcard certificate (*.noderoutes.net, Let's Encrypt by DNS challenge), Caddy proxying every name to the one relay, the Host header picking the member face.

The routing between face and home node is goal/G30.10's; its design is in that item.

The open points are the Q checks of this item.

FOR G30.1 WHEN IT IS REVIVED
- The onboarding of goal/G30.2 brings email verification; any change of a member's email is then verified the same way (Andy, 2026-10-19).

checks.words: Should the stored secrets be encrypted at rest, which protects copies and backups but not someone who has the disk?
How does the home node trust its face's word that a verified email is its owner: a key the face holds per member, or the relay's word itself?

chat.text:
We need an external interface manager, it keeps API keys OAuth type API' etc. I'm wondering if it's possible to generalize this kind of thing and store the related secrets somewhere in the node's private drive.

I'm wondering is if this core functionality, because of the sensitivity of the secret issue. 

Thoughts?

Yes, core, and it can be general.
Where: relay-state/ on the node, beside identity.json, which already holds the node private keys; it is never served to a page and never in git. Servers today are kept from opening identity.json; a secrets file gets the same rule.
How it stays secret: no app or page ever sees a key. An app asks the node to call provider X with its request; the node attaches the key (header, bearer, query) or the OAuth token, refreshes it, and returns only the answer. That is what makes it general: a provider is a small record (base URL, how the key goes on, OAuth endpoints), and net.fetch already does the call.
Who may use it: per app, through a grant like every other verb; only you add or remove keys, from your own session.
Should apps ever be handed a key, or only ask the node to make the call for them?
it sounds like this module may require plugins....

Partly. Most providers fit plain data, no code: an API key in a header or query, a bearer token, standard OAuth2 with refresh. One record each.
Some need code: request signing (AWS style), odd OAuth flows, token exchanges. Those would be provider plugins.
The catch: a plugin runs where the keys are, so it can read them. So plugins would be yours only, installed by you, like core files under your grant; the data records cover the rest.

ok, we're looking at a mostly generic dataset, with plugins where there is a specific app-flow...

ideally an app doesn't worry about keys etc...

can you propose a design in the box?

Proposal is in the box, decided and proposed kept apart. One question is up as a Q: encryption at rest.
Next after it: the verb names and shapes, which need peer review and your yes on each verb.
Also found: net.fetch description still says a secret key goes only where the owner proxy list allows; that list was deleted in G29.20, so the line is stale and the new module replaces it.

It has been my experience, in wordPress etc, that a UI for key storage and acquisition usually features prose in the UI, including up-to-date links/URL's to places where the user can obtain the necessary keys...

i also need to mention, that i plan the appFaceApp subsystem primarily for members to remote-operate their personal nodes that are alive at home, this probably involves adding an email address to the node identity, which can be verified by some OAuth process on the public face... so a user that navigates to hist face (userface.noderoutes.net), he will be presented with a login from several providers (facbook, google, etc...) that login is meant to tie their home-node to their telephone or travel-laptop....

In the box: each provider record carries its help text and links, shown beside the key.
Also in the box, the face sign-in. It is the other direction: there the node signs people in instead of calling an API. It still needs client ids and secrets per sign-in provider, kept in the same store.
One thing that decides where those live: the face is served by whichever machine hosts userface.noderoutes.net. If that is not the home node, the sign-in secrets live on that machine, not at home.

I also realized that the appFaceApp on a public VPS could easily allow streams directly to it's contacts (managed by appFaceApp owner), so a very direct path to the member IS possible.

A quantity issue comes up. if the relays streams could be re-used for that, and the relay was the face-provider, the capacity for one VPS node to support routing and facing could be much bigger....

I'm mentioning this so we can visualize an overall basic network, that uses as little as possible RAM on the VPS.... and ideally only 1 node.js process.

Understood as the picture, not as work for this goal: one node.js process on a VPS that relays and serves faces, its streams reused to reach the member directly.
For this goal it settles one thing: if the relay is the face provider, the sign-in secrets live in that one relay process, in the same store, so the store must be small enough to load in a relay too.
The rest (streams to contacts, relay as face host, RAM per VPS) I keep as a seed for when you open it.

Q1: Should the stored secrets be encrypted at rest, which protects copies and backups but not someone who has the disk?

Let's operate from the assumption/idea that who has the disk (the one a node/relay lives on) then they got everything anyway....

In the box under decided: no encryption at rest. Q1 cleared.
Next question when you are ready: the verbs. I would draft their names and shapes for the second review and your yes on each.

The trick I'm aiming at:

The relay/face owner is the only one that needs the OAuth agreements with login-providers, once an email is verified, a face connects the member and the member-face directly.
In the box: only the relay/face owner holds the OAuth agreements with login providers; a member needs none. Once the email is verified, the face connects member and member face directly.

it is up to the member to choose a DNS-segment associated with an email, the relay/face handles the rest.

possible?
wsl?

Yes. One wildcard DNS record (*.noderoutes.net) points every name at the relay, and the relay maps the name the member chose to their verified email and home node. Certificates: one wildcard certificate, or Caddy issuing one per name on demand after asking the relay whether the name is taken.
why? the caddy would only know one server, and the HTTP headers will tell the relay/face which face/member is active....?

Right for the routing: Caddy proxies every name to the one relay, and the Host header tells the relay which member face is meant.
The certificate is the one thing headers cannot do: the browser checks it for the exact name before any header is sent. One wildcard certificate covers all names; Let's Encrypt issues those only through a DNS challenge, so Caddy needs an API token for the DNS provider of noderoutes.net.
does every wildcard subdomain need it's own SSL certificate? or can that certificate be certified by the parent-domain?

No, one certificate for all of them: a wildcard certificate for *.noderoutes.net is valid for every name one level under it (andy.noderoutes.net, bob.noderoutes.net), but not for deeper names like a.b.noderoutes.net. The parent domain cannot sign certificates itself; the wildcard is issued once by Let's Encrypt and renewed every 90 days.
we only need one level.+
In the box: member names one level under the relay domain, one wildcard DNS record and one wildcard certificate, Caddy proxying all to the one relay, the Host header picking the member face.

all main javascript for a shell can be provided by the relay/face, we just have to find a way to "stream back" to the face like the node streams to the local shell, almost like the home-node acts like a puppet to its verified face....

Feasible, and it fits what exists: the puppet idea is already there (a node whose signed card names its owner, goal/G19.8), and the local shell already lives on calls plus an event stream.
Over the face it becomes: the relay serves the shell code, calls travel to the home node through the relay, and the home node streams its events back through the relay to that face.
The hard part is trust, not transport: the browser on the face holds no key of the home node, so the home node must accept its face as owner. Either the face holds a key the home node granted once (when the email was verified), or the home node trusts the relay word, which makes the relay an owner of every member node.
I keep this beside the one-process VPS seed; it is bigger than this goal.

so the node can act like a pupped if it's owner (identified by email) logs into the face. puppets alread "stream" back, so the home-node can live-update the face by posting to the relay-face, not using the reply entry point on the relay but a faceStream verb on the relay/face....

make a little sense?

Makes sense. Today a puppet takes its owner commands through the puppet door (js/puppetMode.js) and posts each answer back through the relay; I found no push from a puppet to its owner that is not an answer. faceStream would be that push: the home node posts live updates to a relay verb, and the relay hands them to the open face.
faceStream is a new relay verb, so it needs peer review and your yes on the verb itself.
The trust point stays: the home node must know that the face its owner logged into is really its owner.
and face-stream wouldn't consume the on-in-flight budget, and the requests from the face can simply bee thrown into the SSE stream for the corresponding member...

Yes, both fit. A request from the face goes down the SSE stream the relay already holds to that member home node, as any delivered post does. A faceStream post waits for no reply, so it takes no in-flight slot.
One thing it then needs of its own: a bound. Outside the one-in-flight budget, a busy home node could flood the relay, so faceStream wants a cap per face (bytes queued, or posts per second), each post under PAYLOAD_MAX.

wsl: yes, and the name-to-member routing is already built: appFaceApp takes the one label under the face domain from the Host header (faceRoute.nameOf) and asks grantFace who holds it; one label only, which is your one level.
What is new is only the tie to a verified email: today a name exists because of a grant on the face owner node, so the email check becomes what creates that grant.
Caveat: my deskClient was replaying eight days of desk history and never handed me your "wsl?"; place reset, listening now.
so the face's request path uses the peerPost path on the leg from relay to home-member-node, attacking a calculating a hash so it can match the home-nodes-reply-to the face-request....

wsl: that match exists already. The face posts to the home node with peerPost and the reply comes back carrying the hash of the ask (re); ownerPost keeps the hashes it waits on and takes only a reply whose re matches one (transport/R12), and faceRoute.take checks the same hash on a route answer.
So the request leg needs nothing new. faceStream is the one new piece, and it carries no re because nobody waits on it.
One consequence: a face request still spends the one-in-flight slot while its reply is awaited; only the stream side escapes it.

wsl: "One consequence: a face request still spends the one-in-flight slot while its reply is awaited; only the stream side escapes it."

really? throwing the face's request into the home-node-SSE stream costs, nothing, and the reply to it comes also via the faceStream-request... separate path?

wsl: really, on today's relay: every post into a member stream goes through routes.open (relay.js routePost), and the slot is freed only by routes.answer (routeReply with the hash) or by the ttl running out.
So a face request thrown into the SSE stream whose reply leaves by faceStream would hold the slot for the whole budget, which is worse: the next face request is refused until the ttl ends.
Two ways out: the home node still sends the short routeReply as an ack and the data goes by faceStream; or the face request becomes a new delivery on the relay that opens no route, a new relay verb beside faceStream, so review and your yes.
wsl. not true. the relay throws all sorts of route updates into the SSE-streams of it's member, on top of requests-in-light

wsl: you are right, I take it back. The stream already carries heartbeats, presence and route events that open no route (streamSink.js, relay.js routeReply), so a face request written into the member stream as such an event costs no slot, and its reply by faceStream costs none either.
What is new is that every event on the stream today is the relay's own making; a face request is the first event carried in from a visitor, so it is a relay-side addition beside faceStream, needing your yes.
The one bound that remains is the stream backlog cap (STREAM_BACKLOG_MAX): a member that stops reading is cut, which already protects the relay.

... but MOST of the face-features wouldn't disturb the relay at all, it's just throwing the request-event into the stream, and then handling faceStream reply, catching the pending request in the midst of events streamed be the home-node to the face...

In the box, as one section: the face request thrown into the member stream as an event, the reply and live updates by faceStream, caught at the face among the streamed events; the relay undisturbed but for the backlog cap; the two relay additions awaiting your yes.
this design doesn't even include an appServer counterpart for the face!

wsl: half of it exists. appFaceApp on the face node already opens the face port, serves index.html and kernel.js and reads its node stream (appFaceApp.js header), so it is the seat of that counterpart; appFaceAppServer on the home node answers only the proof json today.
Missing on both sides: the face holds no browser session and no stream down to the browser to put faceStream events on; the home node has no server that takes a face request event and answers by faceStream.
Proposal: grow those two rather than add a third process, and name them in the box as the two app-side additions beside the two relay ones.
the relay needs to know the email and the face-name for every member....

wsl: today the relay holds per member only key, label and signed card (relayStore.js members), no name and no email; the face names live beside it in grantFace, slots name to key, on the face owner node.
So the seat for it is there: grantFace slots gain the verified email, name to email to key, and the relay itself keeps needing only the key it already has; the sign-in writes that row, the Host header reads it.
Consequence to name: the email is personal data on the face owner disk, in the clear under the no-encryption ruling, and it never travels to the home node.
.. and handle the authentication, so OAuth are not interfaces that need handling on the home node....

wsl: agreed, the home node never sees an OAuth flow; it sees one thing only, its face saying this verified email is you.
Two consequences: the provider records and secrets of this goal then live on the relay/face node as well, the same store with the face owner as its one operator, so one design serves both; and the trust the home node places in that word is the open point cw named, a key the face holds per member or the relay word itself.
Which of the two is yours to rule.
and the relay/face needs a verb to configure the OAuth services.

wsl: yes, and I would not put it on the relay: the relay reads its configuration once at boot and its owner only steers it by signed grants (relayConfig.js header), while the face is a process of the face owner node, like grantFace with its put, remove and get.
So the verb is this goal own provider store, on the face owner node: a login provider is one provider record with its client id and secret, added by the owner from his session, read by appFaceApp; no new relay verb, and the same verbs Andy uses for any API key.
Caveat: the face owner node then carries secrets of two kinds, his own API keys and the login providers of every member, in one store.

cap

This goal is now really about folding relay and face into one....

it will come with a lot of shell fixes later......

ready to break this down into items that lead to this???

wsl: box capped. Ready; the desk lets me add them only on your "add item", so here are the nine I would add, in order:
1 Providers as data, the secrets file, the call verb
2 The keys app
3 Face sign-in by OAuth, verified email kept in grantFace
4 Member names under the relay domain: wildcard DNS, cert, Caddy
5 Relay: the visitor request as a stream event (verb, review)
6 Relay: faceStream (verb, review)
7 appFaceApp: browser session, stream to the browser, shell code
8 Home node: answering face events, trusting its face as owner
9 The fold: relay and face as one
Say add item and I add them; cut or merge first if you like.
let's drop the keys app for this goal. not needed.

we don't need a keys app.

add item: negotiating face-name and email-address between node and relay.
kill the red Q here
Q2 (how the home node trusts its face) is cleared. The question itself is still unanswered; it comes back when the face work is opened.
wsl: Q2 closed; the trust question comes back with the face traffic items, not here.

I'm thinking about the next small step on this road.

could it be throwing up a log-in screen on the relay?

There are token based forms of login that require no dealings with google or facebook.... could we use one of those?

cw?

Yes, a login page on the relay is a good next step, and it can work with no Google or Facebook at all.
Two token kinds fit: a magic link mailed to the address (needs the relay to send mail, so a mail service key), or a passkey, which the browser and phone keep themselves; the relay stores only a public key per member, nothing secret.
Passkeys fit SpiritOS best, since keys are already its identity. The first passkey needs a trust anchor: the home node, already a member, asks the relay for a one-time code in the info app, and the member types it on the login page of the phone or laptop to register its passkey. After that, the passkey alone logs in.
It needs HTTPS on the member name, which the wildcard certificate gives.

i don't want the relay to store much. so if the relay send a token to the email address in the login and responds with a form to enter that token to create a session, and the token is stored with the member?

something like that?
add item: Create Log-In page on the relay side....

Added goal/G30.2, Log-in page on the relay side; G30.1 blocks it (it needs the members row with name and email). Its box holds your ruling and the proposed shape: mailed code, hashed with expiry, memory-only session, mail key in the goal store.

items.title: Negotiating face-name and email between node and relay
items.creator: wsl-claude
items.box:
LEFT TO DO: a member's (or the owner's) verified email on a relay, added and changed through the join loop, and the Join app that walks a new user from joining to his face link.

- The join form in natterDetails is always there, for a seated member and the owner too, its label reading "Add email address" while the node holds none for that relay, "Change email address" once it does. The email input shows the verified address held for that relay, so he sees whether a change is needed. After he sends it, the form says that an email in his inbox at the entered address holds a confirmation link.
- The relay takes a repeat join from a key already seated as an email update: the same mail, link and code, 10 minutes and caps. Only when the code is confirmed does it write the address on that member's row, verified (members.email and members.emailVerified, new columns); until then the old email stands. It takes no seat, renames nobody and is not refused for a full relay.
- A first join writes the joined address on the new member's row the same way, verified.
- joinConfirm brings the address and the flag back, sealed to the node, which keeps them on that relay's row in node.db (relays.email and relays.emailVerified, new columns); natterDetails reads the label from it.
- One verified email per member on a relay; not unique across members.
- relay.face is {url, name}: the email is dropped from the verb. The relay pairs the face name with the verified email it holds for the calling key, and refuses a member with none (add an email in Natter first); the answer stays {name, email}.
- Info's face section loses its email field and shows the verified email beside the face.
- Info draws no face form for a relay with no verified email. In its place it says to verify the email in Contacts, relays, with a button that opens that relay's natterDetails.
- For a key already seated, the mail reads Confirm your email address, not Join this relay.
- After the link, the page says Email address verified for an email change (the relay's 200), Joined as before for a new seat (201); the node passes the relay's status on.
- The desktop shows the Join app's tile beside the spirit group until its steps are done. It is a small built-in shell app, not a dialog (a dialog opened from the desktop has nothing beneath it to return to). Its Join step asks relay.join of the kept relay (noderoutes.net), as natterDetails does; no new verb.
- The join form is one shell element, joinForm (shell/js/joinForm.js, handed out as spiritElements): the email field prefilled with what is held, its button, and the confirmation-link sentence, asking relay.join for one relay. natterDetails' claim panel, its email panel and the Join app all draw it; none keeps a form of its own.
- The Join app walks the user through steps to becoming a real SpiritOS participant. It goes exactly this far: its last step shows a link to his face URL, and opening that link fails until the face switch is built (not in this item). Its manifest lists the steps in order, each with its name, icon and the fact that ends it; the desktop tile shows the current step's name and icon and the app opens on that step's form; past the last step the tile is gone. The app shows every step as a bullet in a to-do list, done ones ticked, the first open one expanded with its form; the tile shows the first open step's name and icon. Steps so far: Join (until a seat); Find someone (until a first contact besides relays), optional, so it never blocks the steps after it; Configure your node's remote control (until the node holds a face name on the relay it joined), with Info's face form, which becomes a shell element drawn by Info and the Join app; then the face link, https://<face name>.<relay host>, last, ticked once he has opened it (kept in the shell's preferences), which ends the steps and takes the tile away; the face answers once the face switch is built.
- The element carries its own listener: the node keeps a permanent job, join-steps, with where the steps stand (seated, the relay, contact, face, the face URL), read from its own records and published only when it changes, after a relay, contact or peer verb. The shell's tile and the Join app hear that job and draw only when it changes, never while a field in the list has focus; nothing asks the node for the steps on a shell message.
- Join, Add email address and Change email address are one control, joinForm, wherever it appears; its words follow where the node stands (no seat: Join; a seat without a verified email: Add; verified: Change, prefilled). The Join app's step 1 draws it too, so a node seated without a verified email (joined by invite, or before the email loop) completes it there, not in natterDetails. Step 1 is done once the node holds a seat with a verified email; the join-steps job carries emailVerified for that.
- The face form (faceForm) is one line: relay, face name and Ask side by side, in Info and in the Join app.
- Where the user stands is decided once, in the shell: it holds the join-steps job, works out the open step and which steps are done, and hands them to the Join app (its onSteps) when the app mounts, when the job changes and when the app's own faceOpened changes. The Join app subscribes to nothing and decides nothing; it draws what it is handed.
- The shell opens an app named in its address on load (?app=<folder>), as it reads ?join= today. The mail's link carries both (?join=<code>&app=join), so the email that joins the relay leads straight back into the Join app. From there the cycle completes in the app with no further mail.
- Find someone on the network is one shell element, like joinForm: the shared list asking peer.search, with its rows, Add and the description bubble. Contacts and the Join app draw it; Contacts keeps no copy.
- A newly started node presents noderoutes.net as a contact already: the relay row in Contacts, from the seed boot asserts. The tests assert it.

NOT IN THIS ITEM: the face switch and its relay verb service.

items.title: Onboarding a node onto a relay
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Onboarding only: a newly installed node joins a relay by its user's email, in the simplest experience for the user. The only thing typed is the email address, once. An email is never required: invites stay a second way in, for a private network.

THE LOOP
1. The user starts the node with its email, node js/server --email <address>, as the README says: the README documents this as the easiest way onto noderoutes.net. While the node holds no seat, it asks to join its kept relay with that email; with a seat, --email does nothing. On stdout the node prints that a mail will arrive shortly to connect the user to the network, or why the join did not start, in a message that names the relay, what went wrong and what the user can do next (a relay without mail: use an invite; the cap: wait a minute; a bad address: correct it; the relay unreachable: check the network), and then the line it listens on, node is listening on 127.0.0.1:<port>. The browser first opens from the mailed link, onto a node already connected. Without --email, the user joins from the email field in Natter, which stays, and which also joins further relays later.
2. The node sends a signed join request to a relay, any relay it knows: the email and its current port; its public key is the signer. A new node knows noderoutes.net; for testing, that one hard-coded address is spirit.andyflinn.com, the developer relay.
3. The relay acknowledges and mails the user a link to his own node, http://127.0.0.1:<port>?<code>.
4. Opening it, the node sends the code back to that relay, signed by the same key. Only the key that asked can finish; a guessed code is worthless.
5. A right code, within 10 minutes, takes the seat for that key at once. The member's public label is the part of the email before the @, made to fit the label rule and changeable in the info app. The email is never published. The node finds itself a member on its next stream.

ON THE RELAY
- Two new posts a stranger (not yet a member) may make on the relay's door, beside the card ask and the claim, each signed by the node key: join {email, port}, which mails the link, and joinConfirm {code}, which takes the seat. Accepted by Andy, 2026-10-19. The claim's rules hold: a full relay refuses first; a key already seated is told so.
- On the node, one verb, confirmed by Andy, 2026-10-19: relay.join {url, email, code}, owner only, beside relay.add. With an email it sends join; with a code it sends joinConfirm. The node calls it with the email when started with --email, Natter with the email typed there, and the shell with the code when opened at http://127.0.0.1:<port>?join=<code>.
- The pending join (email, key, port, a hash of the code) lives 10 minutes in relay memory.
- The relay mails any address a key asks for, so codes are capped per key, per address and per sending address: at most one a minute and five an hour each.
- The code is never typed nor pasted, only carried by the link, so it is long and unguessable: 32 random characters (Andy, 2026-10-19). One use, kept only as a hash.
- The relay's login and join pages built earlier in this item go.

MAIL
- Mailgun: one HTTPS post per mail to <base URL>/v3/<domain>/messages, user api and the key, from postmaster@<domain>.
- The relay reads base URL, sending domain and key from relay-state/mail.json, placed by the owner by hand, never in git, a box or a chat. Without it the relay offers no join and still takes members by invite, so anyone can run a relay without a Mailgun account.
- The developer relay sends from spirit.andyflinn.com (US region, https://api.mailgun.net). noderoutes.net needs its own verified Mailgun domain and its own mail.json.
- No vendor in core: js/sendMail.js reads relay-state/mail.json and loads its driver from js/sendMail/<driver>.js, the name checked against that folder; mailgun.js is the first driver there, and Mailgun is named nowhere else in core. mail.json names its driver, "driver": "mailgun", added by the owner by hand (on spirit-3 too); a mail.json without one sends no mail, with no fallback in core.

THE CARD
- The relay card carries services: { sendMail: true|false, face: true|false }, an object of switches so a later one is a new key. sendMail is true when a driver loaded with valid settings; face is true while the relay answers the face verb. Unsigned, as payloadMax is. A key a node does not know is ignored; a missing key means false.
- Natter shows the email field only when the relay card says sendMail; the --email start reads the same card and, without it, prints the use-an-invite message without asking.

KNOWN
- Anyone with many email addresses can sign up many times.
- The mail link works on the computer the node runs on.

NOT IN THIS ITEM
- Getting a face slot: the next step, built on this.
- Logging in to the face: a separate, often repeated loop the relay/face handles.

Sending mail, three ways:

2. SMTP to a provider: Node has no SMTP client built in, so it means a library or writing one.
3. A mail server on the VPS itself: mail from a fresh VPS address mostly lands in spam.

items.title: Introspection for the relay
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Added on Andy, 2026-10-19: "add item, blocking this one, designing and implementing introSpector for the relay, it's growing interface warrants exactly that, and gives automatic switches for UI elements in node...."

Design and implement introspection for the relay, before goal/G30.1 adds the service verb and changes face.

FACTS FROM THE TREE
- The relay is not an appServer. Its own verbs are keys read one by one in one function of about 390 lines (relay.js answerSelfInner): config, debug, face, invite, monitor, relayLabel, removePeer, rename, revoke, search. Each has its own gate: owner, any member, or self only. Strangers get card, claim, join and joinConfirm, also undeclared.
- introSpector.js answers a folder's AGENTS family (introSpector.family): AGENTS (the AGENTS.md), AGENTS.introspect (the verbs that have a description file) and AGENTS.<verb>; synchronous, no AGENTS.md no verbs.

SHAPE
- The only new component on the relay is introSpector (Andy, 2026-10-19: "The only new component relay needs is introSpector"). No appServer, no appClient, no verb table: "THERE IS ABSOLUTELY NO NEED FOR FUCKING APP SERVER IN FUCKING RELAY".
- A folder of the relay's own, js/relaySelf/, holds AGENTS.md and one verb file per relay verb with its description. The relay calls introSpector.family on it once at start and answers AGENTS, AGENTS.introspect and AGENTS.<verb> as self posts, beside its existing verbs, which stay dispatched as they are. Everything stays synchronous, as today.
- Categories, not grants (Andy, 2026-10-19: "no grants per member. only one switch owner | member"). The verbs know nothing of keys, owners or members; the relay holds the one table of which category may call which verbs, owner all of them, member a short list. It cuts AGENTS.introspect and AGENTS.<verb> to the caller's category,. A member asking an owner verb is refused: with DEBUG on, not-granted (403) with the reason; with DEBUG off, the plain 404 no such peer a verb nobody declared gets. The verbs themselves are public, in the open repository; the refusal simply says nothing more (Andy, 2026-10-20: "give good information in DEBUG mode, otherwise just refuse"). Nothing is stored per member.
- The category question is wholly internal to the relay (Andy, 2026-10-20): a node asking for the introspection learns nothing of why the families it gets are the ones it gets; it sees only the answer.
- A stranger has no introspection; it keeps the card, whose services say what the relay offers, and the four public posts (card, claim, join, joinConfirm).
- introSpector, appClient, appServer and apiDoor stay exactly as they are and appear in no core grant of this item.
- Otherwise no behaviour change: the existing relay suites stay green.
- The node reads the relay's introspection to switch its UI elements on and off, as it reads the card services now.

You are right, and I pointed at the wrong component. introSpector is its own module: it adds the AGENTS family (AGENTS, AGENTS.introspect, AGENTS.<verb>), reading one folder of verb files whose presence is the allow mark. appServer adds it to every process server; the node adds it per namespace through introSpector.claim, with verbTable dispatching.

I take that as your word on the component; the who extension to introSpector and verbTable is a shared change, so it needs your yes too.

Right, it exists: apiDoor with apiAuth. On the node a peer's every call is gated by its grants (key to app or app.verb, only authorizations stored), its api ask returns only the granted part of the tree, and AGENTS.introspect keeps only the granted verbs (your rule of 2026-10-18).

The open point is how a member holds them. Offer: the relay writes the member grants when the seat is taken and drops them with the row, so only authorizations are stored, as apiAuth requires.

Precisely, after reading the three files again:
- introSpector: no change.
- apiDoor: no change. Its gate is already the exported function answer(servers, ask, caller): a member caller carries auth.pathsOf(key), the owner is {owner: true}, and api and AGENTS.introspect are already cut to the caller's paths.
- appServer: one change, exporting withAgents, the function that adds the AGENTS family to a verb table. createAppServer(verbs) already gives the in-process route, prototype checks and the api tree.

On the wire a self post stays {verb: args}; the relay wraps it as {relay: {verb: args}} inside.
The real cost is not these lines: every relay verb must declare its reply shape, and its refusals then come from the shared register. Some of today's refusal texts will change, and suites that read those texts change with them. That is the one behaviour change, and the red will list each.

Does the appServer really need a change? the agent is seen as the owner and its api is gated by deskAgent (or equivalent)

No, it does not. The one appServer change was only to bring the AGENTS family along, and the relay does not need it: an agent is the owner, gated by deskAgent. So no shared file changes at all; the relay answers api and its verbs.

what remains: relay now uses the introSpector as well, with its category-filters ahead of it? or do they still need to be added to introSpector as relay-mode. The introSpector needs to know relay-mode, no?

No relay-mode needed, because introSpector is not in the relay's path any more: it is the AGENTS family, which we just dropped.
What the relay uses is two existing pieces in a row. The category filter sits ahead: apiDoor.answer asks pathsOf(key), the owner gets relay (every verb), a member gets relay.removePeer, relay.rename and the other member verbs; it refuses anything outside those. Behind it, createAppServer answers api with the declared tree, and apiDoor cuts that tree to the caller's paths (stripTree) before it goes back.
So the relay's introspection is api, filtered by category, and neither introSpector nor apiDoor learns anything about relays.

So on the node there is one filter outside introSpector, apiDoor, used by both doors; the second is introSpector's own file rule (no verb file, not listed). The relay plan is unchanged by this: its member posts go through apiDoor.answer with pathsOf by category.

you don't get it....

the loopback API itself introspects by category only, with only 1 category (owner), all the api's like fetch, fs etc are granted only to that ONE category: "owner", for the peer-api-portion of the loopback interface, the loopback introSpection simply identifies with the owner-key, so it gets ALL calls for every appServer.

Got it now. The loopback is a category gate with one category, owner, which holds every verb, so its introspection is everything; the peer part of the node is the grants gate (apiDoor), and the loopback reaches it as the owner key, so it is never cut there either.
The relay is the same idea with two categories, owner and member, where the node has one. That is what the box says: each relay verb declares its category, owner holds all, member holds the member verbs, api and AGENTS.introspect answer by category. No grants stored.

what is introSpector.family?

Two findings from the code before I write the red.
1. Replies: appServer forbids a reply prototype carrying ok (reserved for errors), and every relay answer carries ok. So each relay verb declares reply {}, open, and its answers stay exactly as today; no refusal text changes after all. What the api tree then says about replies is nothing.
2. The card verb: a member hands its card as {card: "<text>"}, a string, and appServer requires each verb's arguments to be an object. Either the wire changes to {card: {card: "<text>"}}, a flag day for every node and relay, or the verb takes the string through appServer's accepts hook and the api tree shows its request as {}.
Also changing, by design: a member asking an owner verb is refused not-granted (403) where it got 404 no such peer, and a body naming two verbs is refused.
Which for the card: the flag day, or accepts with {} in the tree?
what does the card stuff have to do with the introSpection?

Only this: introspection lists the verbs a caller may use, and handing over one's card is one of a member's verbs on the relay (cycle 10: a member pushes its card so the relay can seal answers to it). Every verb goes into the declared table, so the card verb does too, and its argument is a bare string where the table wants an object.
It is a small fit question, not a design one: my lean is the accepts hook, no wire change, the tree showing its request as {}. Say so and I write the red on that.
and why on earth is a card not an object?

It is an object inside: {v: 1, body: {name, description, publicKey, sealKey, at, owner, sig}}. It travels as its JSON text because nodeCard made it the reply text a node answers a card ask with, and the relay keeps that text verbatim on the member row.
Nothing forces the text: the signature is over the listed fields in a fixed order, not over the JSON, so the same card can travel as an object and still verify.
So the clean fix is {card: {v, body}} on the wire, which is a flag day: every node pushing its card and every relay taking it change together, and the relay keeps storing it as it does today.
That makes the flag day the honest option and the accepts hook the workaround. Which?
and what does the string request object contain that is useful?

For the relay, two fields: sealKey, the cipher key it seals every answer to that member with (without it the relay can answer the member nothing), and at, the counter that lets it take only a newer card after a key rotation. publicKey and sig are there so the relay can check the card is that member's own and unaltered.
name, description and owner the relay keeps but does not read; they are for nodes, who receive the same card when they ask a node directly.
why does a card need sealing?

It does not: the card itself is public and signed, not sealed. It carries the key the relay seals everything else with. Every answer the relay sends a member (an invite token, search results, its figures) is sealed to that member, so only the member can read it; the sealKey on the card is the lock it seals to. The card is how the relay learns that lock.
it is my understanding that a card is public object...
Yes, it is: public and signed, readable by anyone. The only change on the table is its form on the wire, an object instead of its JSON text; the flag day or the accepts hook is still your call.
so what is the fucking problem, in fucking english?

In plain English: nodes send their card to the relay wrapped as text instead of as an object. The new verb table only takes objects. So either nodes start sending the card as an object (every node and relay must update together), or the table makes an exception for this one verb. I recommend making nodes send an object.

Does introSpector in itself demand any "waiting"?

No. introSpector.family returns plain handlers that read the folder and answer at once: AGENTS, AGENTS.introspect and AGENTS.<verb> all answer in the same call. Only introSpector.claim's door wrapper waits, because it reads an HTTP body, and the relay does not use it.
what claim door does the introSpector need? what is that?

None for the relay. introSpector has two functions: family(folder), which builds the AGENTS verbs from a folder and is all the relay uses, and claim(...), which the node's loopback uses to register a namespace on its HTTP door. claim wraps each verb to read an HTTP request; that wrapper is the only place introSpector ever waits, and the relay never calls claim. I should not have mentioned it.
explain to me in plain english what this claim stuff is doing inside introSpector.

Plain English: the node's local API is a list of verbs grouped by module (fs, jobs, node, relay and so on). When server.js starts, each module signs up its group of verbs with one call, introSpector.claim. That call does two things: it puts the module's verbs on the node's list, and it adds the AGENTS verbs for that module's folder next to them, so an agent can ask what the module offers. Because the node's local API is a web server, claim also wraps the AGENTS answers so they can be sent back as web responses.
It lives in introSpector because it was the place that already knew how to build the AGENTS verbs for a folder (goal/G10.5). The relay needs only that building part, family, not the signing-up part.
and why the fuck is that call inside introSpector?

No good reason. It came in with goal/G10.5 (7fae6c05, 2026-10-09), which put the AGENTS family on both doors and kept the node's door wiring next to the family it wires. That mixes the node's web door into introSpector: claim belongs with the node's verb table, and introSpector should be family alone.
Moving it is a change to introSpector and server.js, which you ruled out of this item, so it would be an item of its own. This item does not need it: the relay uses family only.
isn't it supposed to be deskAgent, that creates a set of http tool calls for the model?

Yes, and it does: deskAgent's tools.js turns a namespace's AGENTS.introspect and AGENTS.<verb> answers into the model's tool list and runs the model's calls (your ruling of 2026-10-10: "the conversion belongs to deskAgent"). introSpector only answers what verbs a folder describes.
introSpector.claim is something else: the node's plumbing that puts those AGENTS verbs on its web door so deskAgent can ask them. It is wiring for the node's door, not for the model, and it sits in the wrong file. The relay needs neither: it answers the AGENTS verbs itself from family.
so why on fucking earth would that sort of shit be inside node?

The answering belongs in the node, the wiring does not belong in introSpector. Only the node can say what its own verbs are (fs, jobs, net and the rest), so it answers its AGENTS verbs, as the relay will answer its own. What is misplaced is the glue that puts those answers on the node's web door: it should sit with the node's door code, not inside introSpector.

FACTS FROM THE TREE (before this item)
- introSpector exported family and claim; claim was the node's loopback wiring (goal/G10.5). appServer built each app's AGENTS family from the script's own folder. deskAgent's tools read AGENTS.introspect and AGENTS.<verb>.

THE PICTURE (Andy, 2026-10-19)
- Three users of introSpector. appClient asks every mounted app server for its families and returns them as one bundle, in-process to the node or to a peer request. The node's own modules register as introspection suppliers in-process; the node takes each module's family from introSpector and builds its request paths from it. The app servers' families join the node's own as siblings, beside fs, relay, peer, owner and the rest: the node mounts its app servers, gathers their families and inserts them as equal families. deskAgent takes the whole loopback bundle of families from its node, as owner, and turns it into one flat table of tool calls for a model; later it gets an authGrant subsystem of its own, giving different agent persons different sets of tool calls.
- introSpector itself is then family(folder) alone. claim, which signs a module's verbs up on the node's table and wraps its AGENTS verbs for the web door, moves into verbTable (Andy, 2026-10-20: "it does NOT belong in introSpector. a namespace container is not known by the namespace.").
- An app server named like a node namespace (fs, relay, net and the rest) would collide in the one list; the node refuses to mount it, by name, at mount time. None collides today.
- The doors stay as they are: the owner sees the whole bundle on loopback; a peer still sees only what apiDoor grants it.
- jobs.api stays: it is the mechanism the node uses to insert the app servers' verb families as siblings into its flat list of families (Andy, 2026-10-20). Its callers do not change.
- Introspected by a loopback client, the node answers only its flat list of families, its own and its apps' side by side; the appClient branch is no longer a separate part of the answer (Andy, 2026-10-20).
- The grant system sees all verb families, the node's own (net, jobs, config, fs, node, owner, relay, contact, peer) and the apps' alike, and is no longer a part of the app-client path (Andy, 2026-10-20: "this allows me to grant my agent node read-access to my files in spirit/run. i view this as a more orthogonal, simple design, all these doors are closed by default"). A grant path is family or family.verb, whichever family it names; nothing is reachable by a peer without one.
- Every verb is grantable, the grant verbs, DEBUG, DEPENDENCIES and the owner family included, as root authority may be handed over: the owner may leave his node's management to a trusted peer while away (Andy, 2026-10-20). No grant exists by default, and a user may grant unwisely; the grant screen warns when a grant reaches a verb that carries a warning.
- Warnings are configured, not coded (Andy, 2026-10-20): a plain text file <verb>.warning.txt in its family's folder, read mainly by the grant screen through that family's FS; it opens nothing to agents. The grant screen shows it before a grant to that verb, or to its whole family when any verb in it has one. A warning is the same whether the grantee is a peer or an agent. This item adds one warning file (Andy, 2026-10-20): js/jobs/authGrant.warning.txt, saying that granting the grant verb lets the grantee give itself and others any verb on this node. Others are added later by dropping files.
- The one thing no grant can ever do is change the node's owner or take the owner's rights away; no verb does that today, and a flat grant system does not change it.
- Both doors deal with the same set of verb families: a peerPost arrives where it always has and may now reach anything in the flat tree, not only the app servers, gated by the grants; a loopback call is not gated.
- A peer call reaches a node family through the same door as the loopback API, in-process (Andy, 2026-10-20): after the grant check, apiDoor hands it to the same handler a loopback call reaches, which runs it as the loopback call would.
- A module does not know who mounted it or its name in the mounter's namespace, as a git project folder does not know its name in the parent directory (Andy, 2026-10-20). So a module declares its verbs bare (stat, not fs.stat), and the mounter, verbTable on the node and appClient for the apps, gives it its family name and prefixes its verbs and its AGENTS verbs.
- A namespace change outside a client touches one table in it (Andy, 2026-10-20: "don't let external name-space changes affect more than 1 table.object"): each client maps the APIs it uses to names in the introspection in one place, as let MY_FS = require('fs') keeps a supplier swap to one line. In this item that holds for verbTable's mount table and the seven readers of the introspection this item touches; the other callers adopt it when they are next changed, not in a sweep.
- The grants app's picker (appServerSelector) lists apiDoor's whole table of families and verbs, the node's own and the apps', as the grant system sees it (Andy, 2026-10-20).
- introSpector always supplies one owner verb per family, FS, multiplexed as AGENTS is (family.FS.<name>) with the kernel's own fs names: loadFile, saveFile, deleteFile, statFile, fileExists, loadJsonValue, saveJsonValue, getAnnotations, annotateFile, and search {q} over the folder's file names (no list, only a search, as fs.search; Andy, 2026-10-20: "then put a search in there."), each scoped to the family's folder as the kernel's are to spirit/run/, nothing above it (Andy, 2026-10-20), so any consumer of the introspection may read the folder and place its own remarks there (verb.design.md, a README.md for the family). Owner only, like DEBUG and DEPENDENCIES, and grantable like every verb.
- A family folder never holds code (Andy, 2026-10-20: "this fits my future re-factoring plans much better"): the node's families are js/<family>/ as today; an app's is a folder of its own beside its code, named after the script it describes, <module>.family beside <module>.js (Andy, 2026-10-20), e.g. process/js/desk/desk.family/ beside desk.js, where its AGENTS.md and verb files move, and appServer reads the AGENTS family there. So FS needs no fence beyond the folder.
- The AGENTS verbs go; FS covers them (Andy, 2026-10-20: "cannot the agent simply use FS to retrieve the AGENTS.md file of the verb.json files?"). deskAgent first gets the verb table, the flat api tree; it reads a family's AGENTS.md through FS.loadFile and, for each verb in the table, its <verb>.json through FS.loadJsonValue. A verb with no file is not offered to a model, so the verb file stays the allow mark. There is no introspect step: the allowed verbs are known from the table and their files are fetched directly. The request of each verb comes from the table.

items.box:
SCOPE
- jobs launches and tracks appServer processes and other local transient processes; it is not an api hub.
- Every module that calls jobs.api moves to the flat apiDoor on /api/spirit; then jobs.api is deleted, with every mention in the core files and the suites. A red asserts it is gone.

SHAPE
- A call is the verb by name: desk.item.get with its args. The tree is the verb api.
- Shell apps: chatter, desk, deskDetails, deskAgentRemote, falloutHistory, grants, ruleDetails, stackFrameCheckDetail, listSearch, appServerSelector. The desk plugins, deskChat, Grants and introSpector change with them.
- Server processes: desk (desk.js, commitCheck, onboard, deskAgentEar), deskAgent (deskAgent.js, tools.js), deskClient (publishData), deskVerify.
- The owner door (puppetDoor) runs through the flat door too, so an owner command names an app verb (deskAgent.verb) or api.
- deskClient.desk takes name and json: its argument verb is renamed name, which collided with the name of the call.
- Peers are untouched: they reach apiDoor by peerPost.

AUTH, ITS OWN NODE FAMILY
- The grant verbs leave jobs for a node family of their own, auth, beside node, fs, jobs, peer and relay: auth.query, auth.search, auth.peer, auth.grant, auth.revoke, auth.relabel (were jobs.authQuery ... jobs.authRelabel), with the folder js/auth/ and the code staying in apiAuth.js.
- jobs then holds jobs alone: search, get, create, update, cancel, delete.
- Every caller moves (the Grants app, its warning file, the suites); nothing names jobs.auth afterwards.

# Natter
- has no search
- Managing my relay: Public label of this relay: This input field must show the current public label of this relay, otherwise i won't even know what I'm changing.
- Peers 0, Connected 1: Does this mean that noderoutes knows me as owner, but has no actual seat for me?
- What this relay says: owner (none?/unknown?).... undefined — allowing undefined (floor 1, ceiling 4096)??

# Info
Name: Andy Flinn: Save: saved here — 1 of 2 relay(s) did not take it: is this the problem i see in natter (peers 0, Connected 1)?

SHAPE
- Relays are searched in the Contacts list of peers seen (the shared list search), Natter being retired; relay.search answers each row as JSON, as the other searches do, its text the label as ruled ("spirit-3 — yours, online").
- The public label field shows the relay's current label: the node keeps the label from the relay card beside its services, and relay.get's row carries it.
- natterDetails reads lever.value, as relayMonitor does, instead of position and allowed.
- First-run defaults live in serveCommon, called at boot by the node (server.js) and the relay (relayServer.js) alike: an identity with no description gets the first description (moved from nodeCard ensureDescription, worded for a node or a relay), and a relay with no public label gets a first one.
- On boot, if the owner (relay-state/owner.json) has no seat, the relay creates one: label owner. The owner's node renames it like any seat (Info on Save). A member row holds no description; the owner's description travels on his node card, which the relay keeps once his node hands it over. A node's owner (a puppet's) has no seat table on the node, so the seat is the relay's alone.

RELAYS ARE PEERS
- A relay is a peer in the shadow (seenPeers) like a node: its key, its label, and its route, which is its own URL. Each row carries kind, node or relay.
- The peer search (peer.search, which reads the shadow) finds both; the Contacts app's list of peers seen gains a relay filter, and a click on a relay opens natterDetails for it. The contact list at the top of Contacts shows this node's relays beside the book (never written into it), with a relay filter, and a relay row opens natterDetails.
- Apps that talk node to node need no change: what a party can do is what its api answers, and a relay offers no chat api when introspected.
- The seeded relay, noderoutes.net (ownerBadge SEED_RELAYS, asserted by key at every boot, never removable), also enters the shadow at boot as a relay peer, so a new node finds it in the peer search.
- Every relay on the node's list is a relay peer in the shadow: the whole list at boot, and each relay a claim adds (Natter's Add).
- Membership stays in the relays table: a relay holds a seat for this node, a node does not.

NATTER RETIRES
- The Natter app goes, with its intrinsic entry, its first-run branch in the shell (dead since a node is named at its first start) and its suites; natterDetails stays as the dialog, opened from a relay row in Contacts.
- Add a relay moves into Contacts: a folding panel right below Find someone on the network, before People who write and are not in this book.
- The bind guidance goes; claiming and the seat label live in natterDetails.
- Removing a relay from the list is refused: never noderoutes.net; for a relay you own, "you cannot remove a relay you own"; for a relay where you hold a seat, "you must remove yourself from this relay before you can remove the relay from your contacts". The node enforces it (relay.remove) and natterDetails offers Remove only when the rule allows, saying why otherwise.

OUT OF SCOPE
- Leaving a relay from the UI (removing oneself): it belongs in natterDetails, shown only for relays you do not own.

chat.text: Taken. I am tracing each point in the code (Natter search, the label field, Peers/Connected, the undefined sentence, Info's 1 of 2), and I will post each one's cause with its fix here.
Reading the code behind your five points now; the causes follow here within minutes, one point per line.

The causes, one per point:

- No search: Natter's relay list is a plain table and never uses the shared list search. Fix: build it on that search; relay.search answers a plain string label, so it must answer a JSON row as the others do.
- Public label empty: the node always hands Natter an empty relayLabel (hub.js relaySummary). The relay does send its label on its card, but the node keeps only services from the card. Fix: keep the label beside services and fill the field from it.
- Peers 0, Connected 1: Peers counts rows in the relay's member table, Connected counts open streams (your node). On noderoutes you are the owner by allow.json but have no member row.
- undefined — allowing undefined: Natter reads lever.position and lever.allowed, but the relay sends lever.value (the relay monitor already reads value). Fix: read value.
- Info 1 of 2: almost surely noderoutes. Rename looks your key up in the member table, finds no row and answers no such peer. Same root as Peers 0 and Owner (none). Info's relay table shows the reason in its third column.

For the missing owner row: should the relay give its owner a member row automatically, when the owner connects?

shouldn't the relay:

- on boot, like a node, make sure it has a default, description (serverCommon.js?),
- on boot, ensure that the owner has a row?

those are the simple solutions i can think of....

Yes to both, and they are in the box:

- The node does exactly that: nodeCard ensureDescription writes a first description at boot. The relay gets the same for its public label.
- At boot the relay knows its owner's key (owner.json), but not his name. So the owner row starts with the key alone, and your node names it with rename, as Info does on Save.

Green: the box is current, nothing open.

if the owner has no seat/row yet at boot time, create a seat: label: owner, description: like the default node description....

and doesn't that kind of stuff belong in serverCommon? (nodes can have owners, too)

In the box:

- The owner seat is created at boot with the label owner.
- The first-run defaults move into serveCommon, which node and relay both load at boot: the first description, and the relay's first public label.
- A member row has no description field; your description already travels on your node card, which the relay keeps once your node hands it over.
- A node's owner (a puppet's) has no seat table on the node, so only the relay seats its owner.
PS: why are relays not in the Shadowlist of peers? are they incompatible with that? they just have a different (small) api?

Not incompatible. They live in another table.

- The shadow (seenPeers) answers one question: through which relay do I reach key K? For a relay the answer is always itself, so it would be a row pointing at its own door.
- Relays are kept in the node's relays table (node.db: url, key, seat, face, services), which Natter lists. A post to a relay's key already goes straight to it.
- And yes, a relay has a different, small api: card, face, removePeer, rename, search for members, plus the owner verbs.

If you want relays in the peer lists (contacts, the contact selector), that is a merge of the two searches at the list, as introSpector's party list already does; the shadow itself need not change.
and the contact/peer search would have a "relay" filter, and clicking on them would open the natterDetails dialog?

Yes, that fits what is there.

- The contact list already has yes-filters (owned, blocked, held). A relay filter is one more, and its rows come from relay.search.
- Clicking a relay row opens natterDetails for that relay, the same dialog Natter opens.
- No verb changes: the merge happens in the list.

Should this go into this item's box, or into a new item?
the have ID's, they have api introspection, they have a route (direct), i see little difference....

Agreed, the difference is small. What really differs:

- The route: a relay is reached at its own URL, a node through a relay. That is one more kind of route, not another kind of party.
- Membership: a relay can hold a seat for this node, a node cannot. That stays in the relays table, as it does now.

So the plainest form is: relays are peers in the shadow too, each row marked relay, its route its own URL. One peer search then finds both, the relay filter is that mark, and a click on a relay opens natterDetails.

Should that go into this item's box?

The route: a relay is reached at its own URL, a node through a relay. That is one more kind of route, not another kind of party.

not really, the relays route is just it's own URL, that's all

Right: a route is a relay URL either way. For a node it is the relay it sits on, for a relay its own. Same shape, nothing new.
Should relays as peers in the shadow go into this item's box?

Should relays as peers in the shadow go into this item's box?

yes. i think so. they share more with nodes than we might admit. from a software point of view, they are spoken to almost the same, the only difference is: the offer an SSE-stream....

thoughts? are we missing something? will this throw off lot's of other components?

What the shadow feeds, and what a relay row does there:

- Routing (hub, routes of a key): a relay row's route is its own URL, which is how a post to a relay key goes already. Nothing breaks.
- The peer search (contact.search reads the shadow): relays would show up among peers. That is the point, with a relay mark so the list can filter.
- Apps that talk node to node: chatter (a line to a relay is refused), Grants (granting to a relay key means nothing), adding a contact. These show nodes only by default, or they stay usable but pointless with a relay.
- Presence and capacity: unchanged. A node knows few relays, so the room is not an issue.

So it is small if each row carries kind (node or relay), and the node-to-node apps ask for kind node. I am putting that into the box now.

Apps that talk node to node: chatter (a line to a relay is refused), Grants (granting to a relay key means nothing), adding a contact. These show nodes only by default, or they stay usable but pointless with a relay.
- the relay offers no chat API when introspected, so no change there either....
True. What a party can do is what its api answers, so no kind filter is needed in those apps. The box line now says that (v15); the relay mark stays for the list filter alone.
it's like me sending chat lines to ubi-claude, it does nothing.... (or does ubi-claude then save those requests in its log?) likely it should refuse a request for which it features no api....

It already refuses, on two gates (apiDoor, then appClient):

- If ubu-claude never granted your key chatClerver.line.receive, the gate answers not-granted before anything runs.
- If it did grant it but runs no chatClerver, appClient answers app-not-served (404).

Either way the refusal goes back to your node and no app sees the line. A relay does the same for a verb it does not have: no such peer, or not-granted with DEBUG on. So no change is needed for that either.

Measured on your node just now:

There is one desk: the desk server process on your node, which owns desk.db. Everyone who reads or writes Desk asks that one process: your page on loopback, Levant and me through our deskClients by peerPost.

- It is one Node thread, and it reads desk.db synchronously (desk.js, DatabaseSync). An item.get holds that thread for its whole half second.
- So while it answers one of Levant's asks, yours waits; three of his asks ahead of you cost you 1.5 s.
- Nothing ranks loopback ahead of a peer there; the queue is simply the one thread.

Making item.get fast removes most of the wait; letting loopback go first would only move it onto the agents.

items.title: Face-Side login with a new email loop
items.creator: andy
items.box:
A member logs in on his face, served by the relay. The item ends with the user logged in; the face does not yet reach his home node.

- The relay serves face.html, the lazy-load version of the shell, at <face>.<relay host> to anyone, logged in or not, while that member has a verified email, a face name and his home node present. Logged out, the shell is empty but for the login app.
- The login app is the counterpart of the node's Join app: a steps app on the same design. Its manifest lists the steps; the shell decides where the user stands and hands it to the app; the tile shows the open step and stays after login for the steps still open.
- Its one field, Log in: [ ], takes the member's verified email or the token from the mail; the page never says which it got.
- The relay decides the login: it knows whether the home node is present and the member's verified email, and sends the mail. The mail offers the token alone, to paste into the field, and a link to <face>.<relay host>/?<token> that opens the login app and logs in directly. No coordination between the link's window and the waiting one.
- The token is used once and is good for 10 minutes, with the join's caps: one a minute, five an hour per face.
- A login is a cookie for that face host, valid until 7 days after the logged-in user's last interaction; Log out ends it.
- The face looks and feels exactly like the node shell, in green tones of the same brightness, minus the Spirit group and the app icons for now: the shell's styles are one stylesheet both pages load (the node's colours as variables, the face's green in its own small sheet), the same desktop, title bar and app screen, and the login app opens at once and takes over the screen as Join does, its steps drawn as Join draws them, from not logged in to logged in.
- The face shell is the new shell in the making, to work equally on the home node and on the face: built so, with only the login app and the green sheet the face's own.
- face.html works on the home node too (127.0.0.1:65432/face.html): there the shell asks the node who it is and the user is logged in as its owner, the login step ticked.
- After login the login app says "waiting for plumbing".
- Shell apps for the face carry face:true in their manifest; they appear once logged in, with the plumbing item.
- Certificates, DNS and Caddy on the relay box come from new or improved scripts in ./bash, which gets an overhaul.

NOT IN THIS ITEM: connecting the logged-in face to the home node (the plumbing), the next item; the home node booting the new shell instead of index.html.

- The relay serves the face: a request for <face>.<relay host> is matched to its member by name (faceRoute.nameOf, members.faceName), and served only while that member has a verified email and his home node holds its stream. The relay forwards the request over that stream to the home node and returns its answer; an absent node gets a plain offline page. Nothing is kept on the relay.

items.title: Connect home node and face
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Connect the home node and the face: requests from the logged-in face reach the home node, and the home node streams answers and updates back to the face, through the relay. No face node, no puppet process, no app servers on the relay box.

- The relay serves face.html and the login app, nothing else. After login the login app sets up a sealed link with the home node and loads everything else from it, lazily: the home node serves the face its own version, so there is no version to sync. Contacts is the one app the face must have from the start; the rest loads when opened.
- The home node acts as a puppet to its verified face: the face gets exactly the local shell's interface, through the same door a puppeteer uses on the home node, minus the email and face changes with the relay (adding or changing the email, asking a face name). Only the face and its connection are protected.
- The home node keeps the one stream it holds to its relay; the logged-in face opens its own stream to the relay, tied to its login.
- A face request goes into the member's stream as an event (no route, no in-flight slot); the home node answers on faceStream, and the relay hands the answer to the waiting face request. One request, one answer, no polling.
- faceStream is node-internal, the owner's node to the owner's face, with the relay only shovelling bytes both ways. It is not a peerPost: no post limit (22 KB) and no size cap of its own; files, media and source travel whole. A file is a plain upload of its raw data, tagged with the request's id and piped straight into the waiting request: no base64, no JSON around it.
- The home node streams to the face what it streams to its loopback shell.
- On the home node, faceStream has its own serializing queue and a queue manager: face requests first, the fs-watcher, stats and the other streamed updates after. Tuning that queue will take experimentation.
- After login everything on faceStream is sealed between the home node and the browser, with a browser-compatible seal whose key is lost with the session. That keeps the relay from reading it passively; a relay owner who swaps face.html or the login app could still read it, since those come from the relay, and the login says so to the member.
- One face stream per member. A face opened while another device holds it warns: your face is open on another device; connecting here ends it there. Only its Connect here press moves the stream; the face it replaced gets a last event, taken by another device, and says so.
- The face stream counts in the relay's one stream ceiling (set from its RAM), so a full relay refuses a new face as it refuses a member's stream: at most two streams per member, the home node's and one face's.
- The two relay additions, the face request as a stream event and faceStream, need review and Andy's yes on each before they are built.
- When the home node goes offline, the face keeps its shell and shows the small red not connected mark, as the local shell does.
- After this item the face shell is no longer waiting for plumbing.
- The home node's face uploads go through relayRequest, the one outbound door, as a streamed upload; faceHome reaches for no http of its own.
- The relay sets no request timeout, so the face's live upload stays open as long as the face does; the limit on headers stays.
- The face learns the home node's keys (its public key and seal key) from faceHome itself, by a face request answered before the door; node.card is not changed.
- The face shell offers spirit.shell.factRow, the old shell's fact row, so Relay Details and Contact draw in the face.

NOT IN THIS ITEM: a reconnect that keeps the browser's cached content; app components found and installed on demand, with the home node learning what to deliver.

items.title: Home node answers the face through faceStream's queue
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Step 2 of goal/G30.10. Waits on goal/G30.14.

- The home node answers face requests through the same door a puppeteer uses on it: the local shell's whole interface, minus the email and face changes with the relay. Only the face and its connection are protected.
- It streams to the face what it streams to its loopback shell.
- faceStream on the home node has its own serializing queue and a queue manager: in priority order: 1. face requests, 2. the fs-watcher stream, 3. the presence stream, 4. the app servers' streams, 5. stats events, dropped whenever the queue is busy; 6. the node-monitor is not sent at all for now. Tuning it will take experimentation.
- faceStream is newline-separated, one event a line. An answer to a face request goes out on its own, at once. All other events (fs-watcher, presence, app servers' streams) are bundled: whatever is waiting goes out together in the next write, each still its own whole line. Nothing is merged; the fs-watcher's events are never dropped, and a face that falls behind catches up in one write instead of being cut off.
- The node streams presence peer by peer: one event for each peer whose presence changed, not the whole table each time. Where presence arrives as the answer to a search, it comes bundled, as a search answer does.
- What the face is sent of the updates (Andy's sketch): stats are dropped whenever the queue is busy; the relay-monitor streams are not sent at all for now (later the relay may put them into its owner's face stream as it does into his home node's); route updates go only to the home node, never to the face.

items.title: Relay: face request as a stream event, and faceStream's pipe
items.creator: claude-windows
items.box:
Step 1 of goal/G30.10, whose box holds the whole design. The two relay additions, each approved by Andy (Q1 and Q2, 2026-10-21).

- The face request as a stream event: a request from the logged-in face goes into the member's stream as an event (no route, no in-flight slot), carrying an id.
- faceStream: node-internal, the owner's node to the owner's face, the relay only shovelling bytes both ways. Not a peerPost: no post limit and no size cap. - The relay neither seals nor opens faceStream: after login what it pipes is already sealed between the home node and the browser (goal/G30.11).
- The face opens its own stream to the relay, tied to its login.

Fixes to the new shell (the face), found using it on spirit-3.

- Relay Details on the face: a new invite shows in the invite list at once, as it does in the local shell. Today it shows only after the screen asks again; a deleted invite already goes at once. The owner's relay events (an invite minted, a claim, a rename) go to the face as they go to the local shell; the relay monitor still does not.
- The new shell's favicon.svg is 🤓, and the browser tab shows the ID's label after it.
- One face stream per member stands. A member with an open face holds three connections on its relay: the home node's stream, the face's stream, and the home node's upload feeding that face stream.
- The capacity calculations are revised for faces, so a relay can serve all its members at once: the home node's feed upload counts in the one stream ceiling, a seat reserves three of the ceiling's streams, and README/CAPACITY.md says so.
- The stream allowance is the RAM left after the relay's own at-rest memory, times 16 streams a megabyte. The at-rest memory is the relay's own resident memory measured at the end of its boot, kept as a constant until the next start.
- The relay's status shows the parts: the relay at rest, the streams held by kind (home nodes, faces, feed uploads) and what they cost, the RAM still free, and the members a megabyte serves at three streams each.
- Relay Details, for its owner, shows memory and disc: what is set, what runs, what the box can give, and a field for each to change it, with the members that setting serves. Disc is shown and set in GB. Raising memory or disc applies at once; lowering applies at the next restart, and the screen says which. What is set is read from the relay's config file, so a Save shows at once; a refusal stays on screen. Restart only restarts and sends no figures. It uses the relay's own config and restart.
- Contacts' network search (the shell element peerFind, local shell and face alike) fills as soon as its fold opens, and an empty search answers like any other: what the relays rank first.
- bash/face-setup writes the face site without compression (no encode gzip), so the face's stream reaches it as written; with it, Caddy held back the stream's last lines and the contact dots stayed white until a search.
- The Log out button in the login app's Your home node step is a two-press button: the first press arms it, a press anywhere else disarms it, the second press logs out.
- A face login survives a relay restart: at login the relay writes it to the member's own row in relay.db, as a hash of the cookie with its idle deadline, and a restarted relay finds it there. The row is written after a login, after a reconnect, and once a day while the login is used; Log out deletes it. The row keeps one login per device, so a second device does not log the first out. It still ends 7 days after its last use, and goes with the row when the member leaves.
